research_limits: The requested NYT archive page could not be read directly. Facts were corroborated with the appellate opinion, contemporary wire reports and the NPS-sponsored historical report; the NYT URL is retained as the user's research lead.
The men disputed the undercover officer's account; the appellate court upheld their convictions. No finding of proven entrapment or connection to Malcolm X's assassination is asserted.
The NPS report supplies the later five-year sentences but not reduction dates or actual custody endpoints. Sentence length is not entered as time served.

No verified custodial institution or facility coordinates were found. Omit institution, address, lat and lng; the monuments and courthouse are not substituted for prisons. These profiles will not acquire invented map pins.

Birth and death dates, incarceration endpoints and time-served totals are omitted where unverified. Historical custody flags describe these completed 1965 proceedings, not an assertion about every later episode in each person's life.
Sayyed's race is omitted because period reports and his family's reported identification differ. His full name follows the appellate caption, including Sultarn.
New York identifies the state of arrest and federal prosecution, including for Canadian resident Duclos. Her return to Canada is described in prose; no political-exile duration is inferred.
Michelle Saunier and undercover officer Raymond Wood are not among the four people whose February 16 arrests prompted this request. They are not added by this batch.

prisoner.name: Walter Augustus Bowe
prisoner.description:
Walter Augustus Bowe was a member of the Black Liberation Front arrested in New York on February 16, 1965, with Robert Steele Collier, Khaleel Sultarn Sayyed and Michelle Duclos in the national-monuments prosecution. The government alleged a conspiracy targeting the Statue of Liberty, Liberty Bell and Washington Monument.

Bowe and Sayyed testified that undercover NYPD officer Raymond Wood had initiated the proposals for violence. A jury convicted Bowe, Collier and Sayyed on June 14, 1965; the Second Circuit rejected their appellate claims and affirmed on April 28, 1966. The National Park Service-sponsored historical report records an initial ten-year sentence for each man, later reduced to five. Bowe's exact prison placement and time actually served have not been established by the sources used here.

cases.convicted: Guilty on both counts by jury, June 14, 1965; affirmed April 28, 1966, United States v. Bowe, 360 F.2d 1.

prisoner.name: Khaleel Sultarn Sayyed
prisoner.aka: Khaleel Sayyed; Khaleel S. Sayyed; Khaleel Sultan Sayyed
prisoner.description:
Khaleel Sultarn Sayyed was a Black Liberation Front member arrested in New York on February 16, 1965, in the prosecution alleging plans to destroy national monuments. His co-defendants included Walter Augustus Bowe, Robert Steele Collier and Michelle Duclos.

At trial Sayyed denied intending to participate in violence and testified that he favored nonviolent demonstration. The jury convicted him and the other two men on June 14, 1965. Their entrapment and other appellate challenges failed, and the Second Circuit affirmed the convictions on April 28, 1966. A National Park Service-sponsored history reports that the men's initial ten-year sentences were later reduced to five years. Sayyed's exact custody endpoints and prison placement remain unverified.

prisoner.name: Michelle Duclos
prisoner.description:
Michelle Duclos was a Montreal broadcaster and freelance writer associated with the Quebec independence movement. Arrested in New York on February 16, 1965, she was one of four people held in the national-monuments case involving Robert Steele Collier, Walter Augustus Bowe and Khaleel Sultarn Sayyed.

Duclos pleaded guilty to smuggling on May 13, 1965, before the men's trial, and cooperated as a prosecution witness. Judge William B. Herlands imposed a conditional five-year sentence on June 17. On September 20, he suspended that sentence and placed her on five years of probation, with permanent exclusion from the United States. The NPS-sponsored history records her subsequent deportation. The precise dates of her release from detention and departure for Canada have not been verified.
